p:
So, currently, we have 2,100 that we have hired. We have 5,520 paraprofessionals operating as subpara’s and in terms of the vacancy

rate, that was provided, it’s 1,324 and subpara’s are available to cover these vacancies on a daily basis.
Could you please just state your name for the record?
Christina Foti.

So, 1,300 you said in terms of the vacancy? So, what can be done you know, this is really a dire situation for the paraprofessionals. Again, we are totally 100 percent committed to raising the pay for the paraprofessionals. What is DOEs plan, you know in terms of this and what can be done given the vacancy rate and the low pay rate for paras?

Yeah, I think you know we do so much around recruiting. We make sure that the paraprofessional uhm portfolio is open as much as we can. We’re connecting with, uh, we have principals connecting with local community members to really try to do outreach there. And again, you know we’re open to thinking about paraprofessional pay raises with the support of the Council.
Is someone else - uh, uh, okay.
No, I think that’s good.

I mean, I just want to be clear about this. I mean, our strong feeling is that until we raise the paraprofessionals pay, which absolutely has to happen. We’re going to continue to face this crisis in terms of the vacancy rates. It affects obviously the students who are most in need, who need the paraprofessionals. So, I can’t overemphasize the importance and our strong commitment to raise paraprofessional pay. I have a lot more questions but I'm going to turn it back over to the Chair, so that other Council Members can ask.

Thank you Speaker Menin. One follow up question about the Carter cases and then - I’m sorry, the due process cases and then we’ll go to Council Member questions. I’m trying to understand a little bit Ms. Vladeck. Uhm, I, I mean, I’m maybe a little biased. I think we have great special education programming. I think you agree. I don’t think that narrative exists. Uhm, but you say there’s a narrative that dissuading people from engaging in the special education program that we have here in the city. And also at the same time that even without advertising

your NEST programs are doing extremely well. You have lines out the door. I’m trying to reconcile those two things and also, if we know that these programs work, which I know and we’ve testified here before. This has been my line of questioning before and it’s in the long term going to save money by having fewer students with those private school tuitions. Why aren’t we pumping more money into schools or programs specifically for students with autism?

Yeah, can I, can I just uh - So, look, I think overall, when we think about what we need to do in special education and uhm, you know making sure that folks know about our programs, we also need to create more programs and invest in more programs closer to home for our families. We see that when we’ve done that, those programs are high quality. I visited one in District 12 quite recently. Uhm, and that also cuts down on something; I’m sure you’ll ask later, which is the transportation of kids from home - from school to home and so, we need more high quality programs -
So, so, we agree.
Closer to home and I’ll add - uh, I’ll ask Christina and Liz to follow up on that but just overall, overarching, I think the investment going forward is, is what’s really critical here.

Yeah, so I - let’s - I just really need us to get clear on this. Number one, Liz just mapped out and it is worth spending time on this. She mapped out what the last 15 years has looked like in terms of funding. We have been operating under a system of policy and process where the New York City Public Schools has been asked to do anything by all costs to settle cases. These are students that never entered New York City Public Schools. We didn’t fail them. So, my question you know and I just want to put it back, have we been operating under all, you know doing anything necessary to fulfill the funding requirements of mandated services? The answer is no. And Chair, I have the deepest, deepest respect for you. When we call our special education system broken, that means are children are broken. That means that educators in the system are broken. That means our schools are broken and I argue to the absolute opposite, that we

are at 93 percent compliance because of the deep competency of our schools and our educators and of our brilliant children. Now, when we have funding coming our way, we are able to do things like create world class programs where kids with autism who come in not speaking, graduate in four years at 97 percent. When we have funding, we open up 11,600 specialized program seats. When we have funding, we hire 500 related service providers this year, 800 special education preschool seats, 20 preschool assessment teams that speak children's languages in their communities. Now, if we want to get to a place where we say by all means necessary special education will be funded, then we will not be out of compliance anymore and we will have competitive options for our Carter schools, for students pursuing Carter schools. So, that is the real story here and we can continue to talk about how quickly we pay our Carter schools or we can continue to talk about how we are a broken system out of compliance or we can make the decision finally to holistically take care of our kids and you know Council Member Lee talked about fair student funding and raising rates. Well, guess

what? Fair student funding never paid - never gave us money to support psychologists, related service providers. We do that locally, right? So, like when we talk about special education, I really just am asking folks join in our narrative about how brilliant our schools and educators are and how a broken larger fiscal ecosystem that we’ve been doing everything possible to make up for. That you’ve been doing everything possible to make up for. We get piece by piece investments and when we get that, those pieces, we make gold out of it for children. But we have to start from the whole and so, that’s the biggest, that’s the answer and I know it’s long winded Chair of when you give - when we have that, we have hundreds and hundreds of children waiting on who wants specialized programs. We have families in China saying that I want to relocate because I heard about this program. We have Denmark recommend- replicating our programs. So, when you give it to us and when the city makes this choice, it is brilliant and so, I would say that we have a deeply functional special education system, a fiscal ecosystem that needs the larger help.

So, it sounds like we’re saying the same thing though, which is, which is that, which is that when we make the investments, we do amazing things and you’ve testified to that. So, we agree. My question is, where in the DOE budget are the investments? It is the right thing to do by our students and it is the right thing to do by our city budget to save money on what is otherwise going to private schools. So, that is the question. Where is the money in the DOE budget? Where is the Administration investing this money?
I think we can’t gloss over that point about the money that’s going to private schools that quickly.
Hmm, hmm.

In addition to the fact that people may not know about our programs, there is a very well funded set of folks in our city who do plenty of advertising and outreach to recruit people to outside programs. That’s why there are kids who never show up in our schools. I switched my kid back out of a very well known Carter school because they gave up on him and a New York City Public High School got him over the finish line. The schools that all this

money is going to and by the way, the provider shortage, IESP cases equals related services. So, we have a provider shortage. Why? Because we went from a few hundred IESP cases a year to almost 30,000 IESP cases a year. So, please when DC Foti talks about the ecosystem, the ecosystem is not just OMBs material online about what money coming to us, it is also the outflow of public dollars for private education that is not accountable. Not accountable for general education standards and not accountable for giving a student with disabilities what they need. And I am saying that with respect to Carter and IESP schools. That’s - that’s the part that we really don’t control but really, $1.5 billion a year, the number of seats that we could create in DC Foti’s programs, nevermind the advertising campaign that we could do, that we do for early childhood, that we could do for NEST and Horizon programs. The money is going out the door and it’s not accountable and we need help figuring out why.
So, is it the DOEs position then that you would like to reinstate the cap for service providers?

No, I don't think that’s what I’m saying. It’s our position that any dollars being spent on special education should be accountable right, so that any tuition money we’re paying, any services money we’re paying, there should be some obligation on the part of the schools, the programs, to demonstrate that those kids are getting what they need. It’s why the tens of millions, the tens of millions of dollars we’re now spending to support IESP students who never wanted to come to public school. All of those dollars, all of those providers are - could be going into our schools and New York State by the way, which decided to take the funding cap off of IESP cases, has never put in a dollar to supplement those costs. We’re paying ten times what the federal law requires us to pay.

Right, so uh, I’m going to - I think we should talk more. I want to get to Council Member questions but there is this question about the cap, which I think the D- it sounds like the DOE can take an official position on and can do advocacy with the Council towards - to the state. If that is a real - one of the elements of the

challenges, of the financial challenges for these due process cases. I’m going to turn it over to Council Member Schulman.

Thank you very much Chair and I just want to - uh, I have some questions about Early Childhood intervention but before I get to that, I want to say since I’ve been a Council Member, I’ve been asking the same questions about the Carter cases and what I do want to say is that I have programs in my district that are wonderful for D75 and for kids in need and we have to replicate those. That’s my position on this. Uhm, so Early Intervention is a critical program administered by the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene that serves children from birth to age three with developmental delays. As children age out of the program, the DOE plays a key role in ensuring a smooth transition into preschool special education services. During the Health Committee Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget hearing last week, DOHMH highlighted the importance of this transition and I would like to get additional clarity around timelines, coordination and service capacity.

DOHMH stated that 81 percent of individualized family service plans are developed within 45 days. What is the typical timeline for DOE to evaluate and place a child referred from early intervention and where do delays most commonly occur?

Uh, thank you for your question. Certainly, uhm, when we think about Early Intervention, that is something we are certainly invested in. We - when we think about how programs have been done in the past and things that we want to rectify, these are areas that we’re really thinking about. So, I want to turn it over to Christina. You want to address some of that?

And I’ll start and then I’ll tag you in. And so, as you mentioned Council Member, Early Intervention, that is a process handled by the Health Department but there is a small but mighty team on my team, the Division of Early Childhood Education, that supports with the transition from EI through the CPSE process. Timelines is something that is managed by my colleagues in DIAL uhm on getting them evaluated. So, I’ll pass - yes, thank you Foti.

Of course. So, as DC Hawkins said, we work very closely with Early Intervention and Early Childhood to make sure that handoff is as smooth as possible for families. Not to be a broken record on this point but again, we’ve been making up for lack of fiscal infrastructure on the preschool point. That means, what that turns out to mean for families, that families is that the handoff from Early Intervention to CPSE needs a personal touch, via the CPSE workers and outreach coordinators that work directly with families. Now, when those CPSE workers have hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of cases, that personal touch is a little different then when a family uh a worker is able to - an administrator is able to work hand and hand with a family. And so, with the recent investments that you all helped to advocate for, Advocates for Children helped and certainly the city, uhm made a wonderful investment in, uh we’ve been able to hire you know 80 addi- we’re hiring 80 additional evaluation teams, almost 47 additional administrators and other essential staff. And so, we thank you for that investment and that is what is

going to make the handover as smooth and supportive as possible for families.

Thank you. So, I have a follow up, which does DOE currently have sufficient staffing and capacity to meet the needs of children transitioning from Early Intervention and how are caseloads managed across providers?

Thank you Council Member Schulman. Uh, the- yes, that is through those investments, that is how we are getting there. Uhm, and we’re seeing our compliance rates increase over time but that hiring is happening this year via the current investments. We’re going to expect to see our numbers look much better and have a very clear - much clearer baseline in the upcoming school year.

Okay. During the Health Committee hearing, DOHMH stated it would follow up on how many staff are dedicated specifically to background clearances for 2K programs. From DOEs side, how many staff are required to support or coordinate with this clearance process. That’s part one of the question. Part two, is there a shared system or database between DOE and DOHMH to track clearance status in real time?

That's, that’s me. Uhm, so very intimately aware of this process. So, we do for our programs require PETS clearance, which is different from independent programs, which go through DOI. And so, can get back to you around how many staff currently support the PETS process that is outside of my division. But we have on my team - is a policy staff, also small but mighty, that actually support with managing as the liaison between the provider organization and the PETS team, if there are any delays. I will say it moves very quickly and in certain situations in the past, we have allowed for some concessions for folks to go to DOI. That is not something we can allow it continually but we do allow - uh we do have supports within my team to support with the process.
And we- I just want to uhm, so, I remember when we had the previous hearing, we talked about getting together with DOHMH at some point, so I want to follow up with you.
I would love that.

And I also want to - sorry Chancellor, I got so bogged down with the

previous conversation, robust talk, welcome to our hearing. I just wanted to say that.
That’s okay, that’s okay.
And uh, that’s it but thank you Chair.
Thank you Council Member and next, we have Council Member Joseph.

Hello, good morning everyone. Happy to see you all. Uhm, I have a couple of questions, so I’m going to go fast because I only have five minutes. Uhm, in the last hearing from uhm Children and Youth Committee, Commissioner, Interim Commissioner said they would be having a conversation with you around foster care youth transportation. Can you give us an update on where that conversation is or are you still having that conversation?
Sure, I’m going to turn it over to Kevin Moran as well.
Good morning Mr. Moran.

Good morning. Uh, Kevin Moran and thank you Chair for your advocacy in this space, it’s so greatly appreciated. We’ve been spending a lot of time talking with ACS about more responsive uh

transportation options for all our students, espec- specifically students in housing and those in foster care. One of the things we found of great success was our rideshare program in terms of meeting the immediacy of transportation. And so, that, you’ll see somewhere in the budget, increase from $12 million upwards of $22 million. So, that service is very much appreciated by families and foster as well. We’ve been sharing that data with ACS, so to inform potentially future procurement on their side to help with the immediacy of transportation. We do think we’ll be reducing routing times in the future drastically but as an interim step, we’ll continue to meet with ACS. We’ve given all the data to do some modeling, so we’ll come back on a more wholesome response.

Okay, we can definitely talk about that, absolutely. Uhm, DC Foti, nice to see you. Uhm, thank you so much. I just want to emphasize about the AIMS program in my district that we opened. I mean, it’s a game changer and you came to the grand opening and you saw parents were crying. A four year old had to

get on the bus at 6:00 a.m. in order to get the services where we’re keeping the services in the community. Thank you to you and your team and we’re opening that building on the weekends for SEED program. I mean, come on, so of course, you know how I am. I am a teacher. I do the grows and I do the glows. Is it a perfect system? No, but is there room for improvement? Absolutely with the right investments and we’ve been making the right investments. And we’ve been making the right investments from the last budget and in this budget baselining a lot of the services that our students need. So, my question is around Pre-K Special Education waitlists. In previous school years, we’ve seen long waitlists for Pre-K Special Education students, for classes and services. There have been tremendous efforts to address the issue with the $55 million restored and baselined in Fiscal 2026. For additional classes, another $70 million restored and baselined in this plan for additional services. How many students are currently receiving all of their mandated services? How many students and ECE students are currently waiting for one or more of

this mandated services to begin? How many of the ECE students are enrolled in special education classes and how many students are on a waitlist for a classroom?

Okay. Uh, thank you Chair. So, I just in my previous answer, I should have pointed out to you that based on the origin- these investments, we have already increased the number of evaluations provided by 600 cases this school year. So, pretty remarkable. Uhm, in terms of uh, students waiting placement, uhm - I’m sorry, let me first give you - uh, we have 62.9 percent of preschool students receiving all of their related services. Again, we do expect to see increases as we continue to hire in the upcoming year. Nonetheless, it is currently at 62.9 percent. 12.7 receiving some of their services, 24.4 receiving none, 50.7 percent receiving see at services. We recognize that this is - uh we agree that this is far from 100 percent and as we receive those additional supports, we will - can ensure you that children will be assigned and will receive their mandated services. Uhm, in terms of uh seats, uhm, we have - sorry Chair. Did you mean through the investment? I

apologize. Okay, thank you. We opened 108 to - uh 802 seats via the most recent investment, making sure that every student with a disability in preschool was able to start school on time.
Thank you.
Can I - I’m so sorry, can I just add uh -
Yes, please.

And just to piggyback and just to add, I believe we have about 100 to 150 students currently waiting for either a special class or integrated setting. DC Foti and my team were working in real time to identify classes we can open even in this year. And then anticipating the need for the upcoming school year, so that work is happening.
So, that timeline, that’s the timeline from now to the school year.
Correct.
Any child being placed in between as the school year -
Yes.
Even if we’re in the middle of the school year.

So, we’re doing it on a rolling basis. So, when we and where we can identify classrooms to be opened, we are opening those classrooms and then enrolling children. Sorry, I didn’t mean for you to run out of time. So, yes, happening in real time.

Okay, thank you so much. Immigrant family outreach engagement, student success centers, community schools. I can go on and why we’re not baselining mental health continuum and what happened to Learn to Work? It wasn’t in the Preliminary Budget.
Okay, so -
I know, fired.

Yeah, yeah, so really quickly in terms of our immigration, immigrant outreach, as an immigrant myself, this is - I’m very committed to making sure that our students who are new to the country and are immigrants in general are protected. Our Principals know exactly what to do if local law enforcement show up. Flavia, I’m going to ask you to address some more of that.

Yeah, absolutely. Uhm, so for the funding that Council provided to support

immigrant outreach, it has been leveraged through higher CBO community, race organizations that are directly connected to families to make sure that they are aware of both the fact that we speak their language, the 12 languages that we have resources available. We also have uhm, enhanced our technology through the Hello app, to make sure that right then and there uhm, we can translate for family. This has also allowed uh, to provide direct interpretation services at school. Uhm and I know you also had - I don’t know if it was a specific question about community school as well?
Yeah. Can you talk a little bit about community schools, where we are, how many do we have, do any providers have to be paid or?

Okay. So, uhm community schools, we are at 419 community schools across the city in all boroughs, pretty much you have representation in community schools across most districts. Uhm, we have done - thank you to Council and also thank you to our leadership support, have really doubled down on our efforts to support contracts registration and payment for community

school. As I had testified here previously, one of the biggest challenges was that community school doubled in number but we had the same or like two people less supporting contract and supporting procurement and everything else. So, you can’t expect the same - you couldn’t expect the same quality of level of support. As of today, the 269 CTLE contracts for community schools that expire in FY25, have all been successfully registered and renewed. We also are working to close out the few remaining amendments uhm and the Comptrollers Office is always on point when those amendments are in for registration. Usually the timeline is expedited. Uhm, so far this year, we have put in the hands of our providers uhm around $52.5 million in payments. We took full advantage also the fact that we could do advances to make sure that we could pay our providers in time and I think the piece that I’m most excited about to is as we know, community school is going into ten year anniversary of the work and what we have seen is that across the board, community school graduation rates when compared to citywide were higher. We could see that even after the

pandemic, when chronic absenteeism is an increase. That rated an increase at the same rate in community schools. We could also see that ELA and math proficiency when comparing community school to non-community school. Community school so higher increases. So, when we talked about contracts, when we talk about accountability, not only are we improving our services and the alignment to those to the Chancellor’s priority, but we can actually say with numbers that this work is creating an impact on our students and our families.

And so, finally you asked about uh Learning to Work. Learning to Work is one of the critical uhm areas we look at when it comes to over age under credited serving those students. We continue to have ongoing conversations with OMB about with respect to the funding needed for FY 2027 and in outyears. I wanted to give Jane a chance to address anything else there when it comes to learning to work.

Good morning everyone. Jane Martinez Dowling. Well, first of all, we just want to start by recognizing that learning to work

has been a cornerstone of support for over age, under credited vulnerable students for many years and we’re deeply grateful to our school leaders, our educators, and our community based partners and many of you up here who have really helped us uh, with the commitment and the kid or student success. At its core, uh LTW is about ensuring that students have the relationships, experiences, and opportunities that they need to graduate with a strong plan and a path forward to long term economic security. LTW is grounded in a youth development framework centered on strong relationships, trust and meeting students where they are. The program funds contracts with community based organizations and those CBOs placed additional staff in schools to work alongside school leadership and staff to deliver advising, work based learning opportunities, and post secondary planning supports. As Learning to Work falls under the Office of Student Pathways. Uhm, we currently serve 9,000 students in transfer schools and several thousand students across YABCs including both full time, evening students and shared instruction students who attend YABC part time.

The central message on this RFP is that it’s going to be a modernization of the program, not a departure from its core values. The relationship of this foundation remains. What is changing is the effort to ensure that these relationships are supported by stronger systems, clearer expectations, and more consistent student experiences across sites which align very much with the Chancellor's priorities. This redesigned RFP also expands access to LTW including additional transfer schools and new Charter transfer schools, allowing more students citywide to benefit from these supports.
Thank you so much. Thank you Council Member Joseph. Next, we have Majority Whip Hanks and we’ve also been joined by Chair Gutiérrez on Zoom.

Thank you Chair and thank you Chancellor and everyone else. Everybody okay over there? Okay and thank you for everyone joining us today. Uhm, I want to start by talking about Holding Harmless. Typically a schools budget is tied to the enrollment and additional weighted space on population through the Fair Student Funding Formula.

During COVID-19, pandemic, the city began holding schools harmless to any enrollment changes compared to their original projected enrollment. Therefore, the projected budget for the year. Originally this process helps students during the pandemic uhm where any cuts to schools would be detrimental. Enrollment at public schools continue to decline with 22,000 less students in our school system this year. So, my questions are does the DOE plan to add an additional hold schools harmless allocation for the schools in the upcoming school year? What is the projected costs of holding school harmless next year and what discussions has the DOE and the Administration had about mid-year adjustments and holding schools harmless after the October 31 enrollment registers?

Thanks so much for the question for something that’s really important to the city. When we think about declining enrollment, we see the impact of that across our schools and specifically, many of our schools who serve the most vulnerable populations and so, we ought to be looking at ways going forward for making sure those schools are sustainable and uhm, and can withstand the impact of

the turning enrollment. When it comes specifically to hold harmless, we are having conversations with OMB about various issues, including holding harmless and I’m uh Seritta, I want to turn it over to you.

Sure. Uhm, so just to answer your question around projections. So, there are no projections at this time to share. A lot of the data that goes into inform the policy but most importantly to inform uhm initial school budgets are not finalized until later in the spring.
So, later this spring, we will have a real number of the projected cost?
Yes.

Okay, uh Chair, thanks. So, then we’re going to pop over to class size and mandate and staffing challenges that relates to uhm my borough. In FY 2027, the plan includes $6 million to support class size getting - getting us really to the meeting the 80 percent compliance under the law and despite this investment, District 31, Staten Island, is only at 58 percent compliance and this reflects, not only the gaps but also the facility constraints and teacher shortages, particularly in

specialized subjects like science and world languages. And so, you know critically, while the funding anticipates hiring 6,000 new teachers, the DOE is not aligned in headcount budgeting, raising concerns with implementation, disability and transparency. So, for me, while meaningful progress is made and while we’re doing what we can on class size and compliance with goals, District 31 is still 50 percent classrooms is about 15- 50 percent classroom size compliance, which is significantly below the 80 percent classroom compliance despite citywide progress. Is there any plan to shorten this gap?

Yeah, thank you so much for that question and the class size issue around the city is something that is very, very important to us as we move towards the uhm, the compliance towards that law. Number one, uhm, we look at - we have our principals fill out a survey about their space needs as well as their staffing needs and we try to match those as much as possible. Now uhm, there is significant, like you pointed out, significant issues or concerns regarding our pipeline and that's our

teacher pipeline and that's where we find that uhm, specifically for high schools and other licensed areas very difficult to sometimes meet those needs. And so, we’ve made significant investments. We’ve hired more teachers. We hired more teachers last year than ever before 3,700 just for just new teachers and we have plans to expand that amount in the upcoming year and I want to specifically around teacher recruitment and getting teachers. I want to uh invite Amy Way from DHR to speak to that a little bit.
Please turn your mic on and state your name for the record. Thank you.

Good morning, Amy Way. Thank you so much for this question. Having a talent pipeline to support all the programs that we’ve been talking about and particularly for the class sizes, really essential. Uhm, we have been investing in different pathway programs, specifically to address the shortages in our special education in math and science, which have been a challenge for us even before the class size reduction. So, this is a place where we’re able to attract new talent into the system. I can say for District 31, we have been

partnering with the Empire State Teacher Residency, which is a way to support for your own talent within uhm within a district and so, that’s been a great partnership with the College of Staten Island and Wagner in your community in particular. So, we’ve uhm, you know we have - we recognize that there are challenges with these shortage areas but we have plans in place to be able to build out that pipeline over time.

Thank you and specifically to address some of the space concerns on Staten Island, I want to bring Aaron back because we have been looking district by district across our city very closely with our partners both at SCA and with our union partners and so I wanted to invite Erin to address some of that.

Yeah so as I had shared before, well, first thank you for the question uhm, Erin Jahant, if I need to reintroduce myself. Uhm, uh, thank you for this question. This is something that we recognize as the next phase of the work as critically important. I do want to point out there was a huge amount of investment in Staten Island in terms of teachers last year and we saw

market growth particularly in the schools that we provided funding through the Schools Up model and Staten Island was at 31 percent in the prior year, so there was pretty significant gains and I think you know we’ve heard from principals and teams down there that the schools have just made tremendous progress. With regard to this space, again, we have uhm- we’re continuing our work with School Construction Authority but deepening that partnership and being a lot more intentional in our approach. We’ve met and again, as the Chancellor shared, we’ve gone through every school that has a space, many of which that are in Staten Island. We’re looking to blend how we’re looking at noncapital and capital strategies to be as efficient as possible and in work with great urgency around this. We utilize results from the principal survey, where principals specifically requested us to consider them for annexes or look at room conversions in their school. That information was driven, drove a lot of the conversations that we're having with SCA as well.
Okay.
So, I’m going to stick around and we’ll talk about the School Construction Authority piece and so, I’ll be back for that but thank you for your answer.
Thank you Majority Whip Hanks.
Thank you.
Thank you. I will now turn it over to Council Member Restler.

Thank you so much Chair Dinowitz and Chancellor and team, good to see you all. Congratulations to all of the new folks in your - or reappointed new whatever official roles you’re all in. Congrats. Uhm, and Chair, thank you for leading this thoughtful hearing. I think it’s really been productive. Uh, I just want to follow up on the uhm, on the Whips questions and the Chair asked about this a little bit as well on Hold Harmless. As Chancellor, you may recall, this was the issue that uh, uh torpedoed the relationships between our previous Mayor and our previous Speaker and I hope that we don’t have similar problems uh in this budget.

My understanding is that the Hold Harmless funds are not generally incorporated at Prelim, so we’re not surprised that they’re not there today but we are concerned. Uhm, you know recognizing we are seeing shifts in enrollments in our schools and there comes a time where we’re going to have to reflect that in our budgets. The average Hold Harmless funding if I understand it right and Ms. Scott, please correct me, is about $280,000 per school. And so, just want to understand - are conversations happening now uh around gradually shifting funding for Hold Harmless amounts? Are we expecting to see full reductions in Hold Harmless funding? I’ve got a great public school PS 261 that receives $66,0000 a year that they depend on critically. I want to make sure that they’re supported. It would be - these could be major challenges for the schools to face if they see a significant reduction in their funding in their budgets in June. Could you give us some insight into how you’re approaching this issue?

Yeah, first of all, uhm thank you for raising the question and uhm, also Council Member
